common_name: Even' Star Ice-Bred Collards (Cold-Hardy Landrace Collard)
scientific_name: Brassica oleracea var. viridis 'Even' Star Ice-Bred'

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting and set out in late summer to fall so the crop is maturing as hard freezes arrive; this landrace was developed by repeatedly selecting survivors of severe Mid-Atlantic winter freezes, so it performs best when allowed to stand through cold rather than being harvested young.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants generously to allow air movement through the dense winter canopy. This is a farmer-bred landrace rather than a fixed variety, so individual plants show some variation in leaf shape and color, a trait intentionally preserved because it broadens genetic resistance to hard freezes. Repeated exposure to temperatures well below freezing triggers a marked increase in sweetness as the plant converts stored starches to sugars for cold protection, so flavor peaks after the first several freeze events rather than at first harvest. Because the strain was selected under working-farm winter conditions rather than in a breeding trial, gardeners should expect a rougher, more variable-looking plant than commercial hybrids in exchange for exceptional cold survival.
sources: Even' Star Organic Farm variety notes

planting.note: Direct sow in late summer for a fall-through-winter crop in mild zones, or start a spring planting once soil is workable in cooler zones; individual outer leaves can be harvested continuously once the rosette is established rather than waiting for a single cutting.

directions: Sow directly in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and thin to a loose, non-heading rosette habit rather than the upright single stalk typical of Southern collard types. The broad, smooth, pale-to-medium green leaves are notably thinner and more tender than typical American collards, cooking down faster and with a milder, almost cabbage-like flavor that suits quick sautes as readily as long-simmered pots. This is the collard type traditionally used in Portuguese caldo verde soup, where leaves are shredded into fine ribbons, so gardeners growing it for that purpose should prioritize leaf tenderness over plant size when harvesting. Because the plant does not form a strong central stalk, it is more prone to sprawling in heavy rain or wind and benefits from a bit more spacing than compact collard hybrids.

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before transplanting; this hybrid's faster maturity and heat tolerance allow an earlier late-summer planting date than open-pollinated Southern types, extending the harvest window on both ends of the season in zone 8-10 gardens.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this F1 hybrid was bred for commercial-style uniformity, producing tall, upright plants with smooth, dark blue-green leaves held tightly on a strong central stalk that resists lodging in wind. Hi-Crop tolerates late-summer heat noticeably better than heirloom Southern collards, allowing growers to set plants out a few weeks earlier in fall and still avoid the bitterness that heat stress causes in less tolerant types. Its uniform growth habit and heavy leaf set make it well suited to multiple-pass harvesting, where the lower leaves are stripped repeatedly over several months while the growing point continues producing new leaves at the top.

planting.note: Direct sow thickly for a cut-and-come-again greens crop from late summer through fall in zone 8-10; a spring sowing before hot weather sets in is also workable since this type resists bolting better than root-focused turnips.

directions: Direct sow into fertile, loose soil in full sun and thin lightly, since this variety is grown for its leaves rather than a marketable root and tolerates closer spacing than globe-type turnips. The smooth, broad, dark green leaves grow rapidly and regrow readily after cutting, making Topper well suited to a repeated cut-and-come-again harvest schedule rather than a single whole-plant pull. It resists the bitterness and rapid bolting that hot weather causes in many greens turnips, giving Southern gardeners a wider planting window than strictly cool-season varieties allow. The small, often forked roots are edible but are not the point of growing this variety, so gardeners aiming for a good turnip root should choose a globe type instead.

planting.note: Direct sow from late summer into fall in the Gulf South; this old Southern strain has been maintained by regional seed savers largely for its leaf quality, so successive sowings every few weeks give the steadiest supply of tender greens.

directions: Direct sow into well-worked, fertile soil in full sun; Crawford is a regionally maintained Southern heirloom kept in circulation primarily by seed savers and small seed houses rather than large commercial catalogs, valued for producing abundant, tender leaves ahead of a usable root. The leaves are typically harvested young and often cooked alongside the thinnings, since the strain was selected on Southern farms as a dependable greens crop rather than for uniform root size or shape. Because it is an open-pollinated landrace-style variety rather than a modern hybrid, expect some natural variation in leaf shape and root form from plant to plant. Flavor improves with cool weather and light frost, following the same pattern as other greens-type turnips grown in Gulf Coast gardens.

common_name: Ostrich Plume Mustard (Heirloom Fringed-Leaf Curled Mustard)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for the mildest, most tender leaves; this old curled heirloom bolts and turns sharply pungent quickly once heat arrives, so it is best treated strictly as a cool-season crop in zone 8-10 gardens.

directions: Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Ostrich Plume is a long-grown American heirloom curled mustard named for its finely cut, deeply frilled, feather-like leaf margins that resemble ostrich plumage more than the coarser curling seen in many mustard types. The tightly ruffled bright green leaves make an attractive garnish planting as well as a cooking green, and young leaves are mild enough for fresh salad use before the plant matures into fuller mustard heat. Like other curled mustards, it is fast to bolt once day length and temperature increase, so successive small sowings through the cool season give a steadier harvest than one large planting. Older, larger leaves develop a stronger peppery bite and are best suited to cooked greens rather than raw eating.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall through winter in zone 8-10; leaves can be harvested as baby greens in as little as three weeks or allowed to mature further for the fuller-flavored leaves traditionally used in pancit and other stir-fried dishes.

directions: Direct sow into fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to partial shade; Amsoi is a broadleaf mustard type long grown in Filipino home gardens and widely used in Filipino cooking, particularly in noodle dishes and sauteed vegetable sides. The smooth, glossy, dark green leaves are broader and less deeply lobed than curled mustard types, with a flavor that is noticeably milder and less sharply pungent than Southern mustard greens, making it approachable for cooks who find typical mustard heat too strong. Because it prefers steady moisture and moderate temperatures, it performs best as a cool-season crop and tends to turn bitter and bolt quickly once hot weather sets in. Harvest by cutting outer leaves or the whole young plant, since regrowth from the cut stem is reliable during the cool months.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources Extension
